entries.meaning: ‘The guru's grace protects your company and ours, home and forest alike. The directions of mother, father, guru, and master are Śeṣa, the bearer of the whole earth of duty. Carry them out yourself and cause me to carry them out, dear brother, and become the protector of the Solar line. That one discipline grants every attainment and is a braid woven of fame, a blessed end, and prosperity. Considering this, endure the heavy crisis and make the subjects and family happy. Destiny has divided the hardship among everyone, brother, but yours is the hardest for the full appointed term. Knowing your gentleness, I speak harshly; in a bad hour my doing so is not improper, dear child. In a perilous place, lovely true kinsmen hold even their hands over one who is struck by a thunderbolt. The servant is hands, feet, and eyes, while the master is the mouth: hearing this rule of love, Tulasī says, the good poets praise it.’

The whole assembly heard Raghubara's speech as though nectar had been infused into an ocean of love. The company went slack in an absorption of affection; seeing their condition, Sarasvatī herself practiced silence. Bharata attained supreme contentment: facing one's master brings happiness, while turning away brings suffering and fault. His face became glad and his despondency vanished, as though by grace a mute person had received speech. He lovingly bowed once more and said with lotus hands joined: ‘Lord, what joy has arisen from coming with you! I have won the gain for which birth is taken in the world. Merciful Lord, whatever command now comes, I shall reverently place it upon my head and carry it out. God, give me the support by serving which I may cross the far shore of the appointed term. Lord, under the guru's direction I brought water from all the holy places for the consecration; what is your command concerning it?’

‘There is one great desire in my heart, but through fear and reserve I cannot express it.’ ‘Speak, dear child,’ said the Lord, and with Rāma's permission Bharata answered in affectionate words: ‘Citrakūṭa's holy ground, places of pilgrimage and forests, its birds and animals, ponds and rivers, waterfalls and ranges of hills—and above all the earth marked by the Lord's feet: with permission I would go and see them.’ ‘Certainly bear Atri's command upon your head, dear child, and roam the forest without fear. By the sage's grace the forest gives blessing; it is supremely pure and lovely, brother. Keep the holy water at whatever place the chief sage directs.’ Hearing the Lord's words, Bharata rejoiced and bowed his head at the sage's lotus feet. The whole exchange between Bharata and Rāma was a root of every blessing; even the self-interested gods praised their house and showered flowers from the celestial trees.

‘Blessed is Bharata! Victory to Lord Rāma!’ the gods exclaimed, rejoicing abundantly. When Janaka, the sages, and all in the assembly heard Bharata's words, enthusiasm arose. Videha's king thrilled as he extolled the clusters of Rāma's and Bharata's virtues and their love. The lovely natures of servant and master, and their supremely purifying constancy and love, moved ministers and courtiers to praise them according to their understanding. Hearing the dialogue of Rāma and Bharata again and again, both companies felt joy and sorrow in their hearts. Rāma's mother regarded pain and pleasure alike and consoled the queens by recounting Rāma's virtues. Some praised Raghubīra's greatness; others praised Bharata's goodness. Then Atri told Bharata: ‘Near the mountain is a beautiful well. Place the water of the holy places there—water unequalled and pure as nectar.’

Receiving Atri's instruction, Bharata sent all the water vessels ahead. With his younger brother, Atri, other sages, and holy people, he went to where the well was deep. ‘The sacred water has been placed in a holy site,’ Atri said joyfully and lovingly. ‘Dear child, this is an eternal place of accomplished power. Time had concealed it, and no one now knew of it. Then the servants saw this moist spot and, for the sake of the fine water, made a special well. Through destiny it has become a benefit to the world, making an exceedingly profound conception of duty accessible. People will now call it Bharata's Well, joined to the water of the supremely holy places. Creatures who bathe here with love and due observance will become stainless in deed, mind, and speech.’ Describing the full greatness of the well, they returned to where Raghurāya was, and Atri told Raghubara the holy power of the pilgrimage-place.

As they lovingly recounted sacred histories, dawn came and that delightful night passed. Bharata and his two brothers performed the daily rites and, receiving the commands of Rāma, Atri, and the guru, set out with the whole plainly equipped company to wander Rāma's forest on foot. When his tender feet walked without sandals, the ground grew soft, inwardly abashed. It hid away kuśa grass, thorns, pebbles, rough ground, and every sharp, hard, or harmful thing, and made lovely gentle paths. Three kinds of pleasant breeze blew; gods rained flowers and clouds provided shade, while trees blossomed and fruited and the grass became tender. Deer looked upon him, birds spoke graciously, and all served him knowing he was dear to Rāma. Even an ordinary person readily gains every supernatural power merely by saying ‘Rāma’ while yawning; that such wonders attended Bharata, dearer to Rāma than life, is no great thing.

Bharata wandered through the forest in this manner, and sages felt humbled when they saw his observance and love. He asked about holy bodies of water and tracts of land, birds and animals, trees and grasses, mountains, forests, and gardens, seeing every place as lovely, wondrous, pure, and special. Hearing his questions, the sage-king gladly recounted the cause, name, qualities, sanctity, and spiritual power of each. At one place Bharata bathed, at another he bowed, elsewhere he gazed with a delighted mind. Sometimes he sat with the sage's permission and remembered Sītā together with the two brothers. Seeing his disposition, affection, and excellent service, the forest deities joyfully blessed him. They returned after two and a half watches, and Bharata came to behold the Lord's lotus feet. In five days he saw every place and pilgrimage-site; as they spoke and heard the fair fame of Hari and Hara, the day passed and evening came.

At dawn everyone bathed and the full assembly gathered—Bharata, the brahmins, and the king of Tirhut. Knowing inwardly that this was a suitable day, merciful Rāma began to speak but hesitated. He observed the guru, the king, Bharata, and the assembly; then, abashed, looked again toward the ground. Praising his character, everyone in the assembly reflected that no master was as considerate as Rāma. Wise Bharata read Rāma's inclination, rose with love, and gathered exceptional courage. Prostrating himself, he said with hands joined: ‘Lord, you have fulfilled every desire of mine. For my sake everyone endured anguish, and you yourself suffered in many ways. Now, Lord, give me permission to go and serve Ayodhyā throughout the appointed term. Teach me the means by which, when the term is over, your servant may behold the Compassionate Protector of Kosala again.’

‘Lord, townspeople, family, subjects, and relatives are all bound to you in pure, tender affection. Without you even the highest spiritual state is wasted, and worldly pain burns more fiercely. As a discerning master you know every servant's way of life, desire, and longing. Protector of the submissive, you will preserve everyone; Lord, sustain both sides. In this I have abundant trust in you in every way, and after reflection no severe worry remains. My own distress and my Lord's tenderness joined together and made me boldly obstinate. Remove this great fault, Master; abandon reserve and instruct your follower.’ Hearing Bharata's plea, everyone praised it as one praises a swan's power to separate milk from water. The friend of the poor heard his poor, guileless brother's words, and accomplished Rāma replied in a manner suited to the country, time, and occasion.

‘Dear child, the concerns of you, me, our family, the household and forest all rest upon the guru and the king. With the guru, sages, and lord of Mithilā over our heads, neither you nor I will suffer even in a dream. For you and me the highest human achievement—personal good, fair fame, duty, and the supreme goal—is this: we two brothers shall keep our father's command, for the good of worldly custom, the Veda, the king, and his renown. By keeping the teaching of guru, father, mother, and master, one's feet do not slip even while walking upon a bad road. Considering this, abandon all anxiety and go govern Ayodhyā for the full term. Country, treasury, relations, and family: when their burden rests upon the dust of the guru's feet, it becomes light. Accepting the teaching of guru, sages, mothers, and ministers, protect the earth, the subjects, and the capital. A leader should be like the mouth: alone it receives food and drink, but with discernment it nourishes and sustains all the limbs.’
